examples: If you ask me, that explanation is inadequate.
From the victims' point of view, the sentence is far too light.
If you ask a teacher, the basics are what matter.
From the parents' point of view, staying out late at night is worrying.
If you ask an expert, the risk is not low.
To be honest, I can't agree.
fields.explain:
Placed at the beginning of the sentence, optionally followed by a comma to mark a pause: 〜から言わせれば、…
Used to signal one's own opinion in advance, preparing for a contrary statement.
In casual speech: 〜から言わせりゃ (colloquial, masculine).

• States the subjective opinion of the agent N, often to open a rebuttal or to "speak frankly".
• Implies "if you make me (say it), then…", adding emphasis.
• Usually used with a person/group as the agent: 私／親／教師／専門家／被害者.
fields.notes:
• Can be combined with emphatic adverbs: 正直に／率直に／あくまで個人的には + から言わせれば.
• Avoid overusing it in academic writing because of its strong subjective nuance.
mistakes: Used with an inanimate noun: ×結果から言わせれば → use から言えば/から見ると.
Confusing the nuance with から言えば: if the question calls for "criticism" → choose から言わせれば.
Omitting the agent N makes the sentence vague: state clearly who is speaking if the context does not make it clear.

examples: Everyone makes mistakes to some extent.
For better or worse, that decision will have a major impact on the company.
Sooner or later, the truth will come out.
Whether it's expensive or cheap, I want to put quality first.
Sooner or later, he will probably be held responsible.
Everyone is under some degree of stress.

Usage: Used as an adverbial expressing a condition that covers both extremes: 多かれ少なかれ、～ Expresses a general or inevitable result/judgment.Mainly used with i-adjectives; some phrases use nouns/nominalized qualities: 若かれ老いかれ .

Expresses a general or inevitable result/judgment.

Nuance: Formal, idiomatic; often found in articles, speeches and the press.Implies "no matter where on the scale it falls, the conclusion still holds".

Do not freely create new pairs if they are not natural in Japanese. Prefer the familiar phrases.
Some words have an almost fixed order: 多かれ少なかれ , 遅かれ早かれ , 良かれ悪しかれ .

• Meaning 1: "Whether A or B, … / No matter whether at level A or B, …"

- Emphasizes that the conclusion does not change at either of two opposite extremes of a scale.

- The paired adjectives are usually antonyms or the two ends of a scale of degree, time or quality.

• Meaning 2: "more or less / sooner or later / near or far / expensive or cheap"

- Expresses universality or inevitability: it will happen or be true within a certain scope.

• Nuance: Somewhat formal, written language; idiomatic. Some very common phrases: 多かれ少なかれ (more or less), 遅かれ早かれ (sooner or later), 良かれ悪しかれ (for better or worse).
fields.notes:
• Origin of the form: "～かれ" is a remnant of an old i-adjective form in Japanese, preserved in some idioms such as 良かれ悪しかれ, 遅かれ早かれ. Because of this history, many phrases are fixed and hard to create freely.
• "悪しかれ": This form is fixed in the phrase 良かれ悪しかれ; learners often mistake it for "悪かれ". Memorize it as the standard phrase.
• Comma: A comma usually follows the phrase when it comes at the beginning of a sentence: 多かれ少なかれ、～ to set off the adverbial.
• Pragmatics: Suited to formal written language, the press and presentations. In everyday conversation, it can be replaced with 多少, いずれ, どっちにしても depending on the context.
mistakes: Wrong form:
Incorrect: 良いかれ悪いかれ → Correct: 良かれ悪しかれ
Incorrect: 悪かれ in the phrase above → Correct: 悪しかれ
Making up unnatural pairs:
Incorrect: 美しかれ綺麗かれ (unnatural)
Prefer familiar phrases such as 多かれ少なかれ, 遅かれ早かれ.
Confusing it with "AかBか" (choice/question sentences):
行くか行かないか ≠ 遅かれ早かれ. The pattern "～かれ～かれ" is not a question or choice pattern but an idiom covering both extremes.
Fixed word order:
Usually: 多かれ少なかれ, 遅かれ早かれ. Reversing the order tends to sound odd in exams.
JLPT answer-choice traps:
Choosing between 多かれ少なかれ and 多少なりとも: both mean "more or less", but if a formal idiomatic nuance is required → prefer 多かれ少なかれ.
Choosing between 遅かれ早かれ and いずれ: if you need an opposing pair/emphasis on both extremes → 遅かれ早かれ.

fields.connection: V/A plain form + (が)ゆえに / N・Na + (である)
examples: Because he was young, he took on a reckless challenge.
Precisely because she is so serious, she is sometimes misunderstood by the people around her.
Because of their fame, even trivial remarks become a big topic.
Mistakes that come from ignorance can be reduced through education.
Because the paperwork was neglected, the payment was delayed.
fields.explain:
Used when you want to state a reason formally or emphasize that something is inevitable/unavoidable.
Can imply "it can't be helped/it was unavoidable" or "precisely because of that, it is deserved".
In spoken language it is usually replaced with ～ため(に) or ～せいで depending on the nuance.

～がゆえに = "precisely because/owing to (an inherent reason)", formal nuance, sometimes with a feeling of justification or inevitability (can be positive or negative).
• Emphasizes a cause-effect relationship based on an inherent attribute/circumstance: 若さ・貧しさ・有名であること, etc.
• Often used in essays, the press, regulations and formal speeches.
• The form ～がゆえのN turns the cause into a quality that modifies a noun.
fields.notes:
• Before がゆえに, na-adjectives/N require である; this is a point often tested in JLPT N1.
• ～がゆえのN is very useful for condensing a cause into a quality that modifies a noun.
• Do not overuse it in everyday conversation, as it sounds affected.
mistakes: Omitting である before na-adjectives/N: incorrect. Correct: 不便であるがゆえに, not 不便だがゆえに.
Confusing the nuance with ～せいで: がゆえに is not necessarily negative; it is formal/academic.
Choosing between ～ために and ～がゆえに in answer choices: when the context is formal/an inherent attribute → choose がゆえに.

rows: Emphasizes a reason based on an attribute
Blaming, attributing fault to the cause
Expresses degree: "precisely because…, all the more…"

fields.connection: V/A plain form + (が)ゆえの + N / N・Na + (である)
examples: A failure due to lack of experience.
It is harsh to blame someone for the recklessness that comes with youth.
A misunderstanding arose because he is a foreigner.
It was a choice born of poverty.
I endure the pressure that comes with being the person in charge.
A misjudgment caused by haste.
fields.explain:
Formal nuance; written language, theses, the press, official speeches.
Emphasizes the "unavoidable" nature arising from essence/circumstances: "precisely because ..., ...".
Often used with general abstract nouns:過ち,誤解,苦労,重圧,決断,行動.
Position: ～がゆえの + N (directly before the noun it modifies).
With ナ形/N: であるが望ましい. Avoid "だがゆえの" in formal writing; use "である".
Not used for overly light everyday expressions; replace with ～せいでの, ～ための in casual contexts.

～がゆえの means "precisely because/owing to ..., ..." and modifies the following noun, emphasizing an inherent cause, with a formal, written nuance.
• Implies "because of that nature/circumstance, ... inevitably arises".
• Often used with words denoting attributes such as 若さ, 未熟, 無知, 立場, 事情, 責任.
• Compared with ～ための, ～がゆえの is more formal, with the nuance of "for that reason/because of that very thing".
• It has a parallel sentence form: ～がゆえに (adverbial). The form discussed here modifies a noun: ～がゆえの + N.
fields.notes:
• "ゆえ" is the Sino-Japanese "故", meaning "cause/reason", so it has a classical, solemn nuance.
• The long form "～であるがゆえの" gives the sentence a firm rhythm and is accurate with N/ナ形.
• In media/PR, it is used to soften the nuance of blame: "誤解がゆえの発言".
• Be careful when the agent is a person: it may sound like an excuse. Weigh the context.
mistakes: Using "だがゆえの" with N/ナ形 in formal writing: use "であるがゆえの" instead.
Confusing it with ～せいでの: if you do not want a strong nuance of blame, choose ～がゆえの.
Wrong modifier position: it must be "X がゆえの N"; do not separate the "の".
JLPT: trap choices between ～ための and ～がゆえの; if the answer requires a formal nuance → choose ～がゆえの.
Confusing its function with ～がゆえに: one modifies a noun, the other is an adverbial for a clause.

rows: Neutral, more colloquial; not necessarily formal
<ruby>経験<rt>けいけん</rt></ruby><ruby>不足<rt>ふそく</rt></ruby>のための<ruby>失敗<rt>しっぱい</rt></ruby>

<ruby>若<rt>わか</rt></ruby>いがゆえに<ruby>失敗<rt>しっぱい</rt></ruby>もある

fields.meaning: If… is like that, then… is too
examples: Like parent, like child.
The boss is no better than the staff, and the staff are no better than the boss.
The customers are bad, but the shop is just as bad.
The manager is hopeless, and so are the players.
The teacher is no good, and neither are the students.
Like parent, like child, honestly.
fields.explain:
Often used to criticize, to be sarcastic or to express irritation; avoid using it directly toward a superior so as not to be rude.
The two nouns should be a related pair (parent–child, teacher–student, boss–staff, customer–shop...).
It does not express a real condition (if A, then B). The meaning is "given that A is the kind of A it is, B is the same kind of B".
The sentence usually ends with だ; よ/ね/な can be added to adjust the nuance in spoken language.

The pattern ～が～なら、～も～だ (as well as the variant ～も～なら、～も～だ) judges that both A and B are "just what you'd expect of A/B" and tend to be similar (usually negative). That is, if A is like that, B is no better; both match each other in how good/bad they are (mostly criticism).
• "なら" here is not a real condition but means "in terms of capacity/character".
• It combines almost only with nouns (roles, capacities, groups of people/things).
• Used as a comment/exclamation, often with a sarcastic nuance.
fields.notes:
• The actual subject can be omitted; it is highly formulaic and common in the press/commentary.
• Exclamatory adverbs can be added: まったく／本当に／やれやれ, but consider politeness.
• Symmetry: keep the same kind of noun (role/capacity) in both clauses so it sounds natural.
• In spoken language, "だ" can be replaced with "だよ／だね／だな" depending on attitude. | Distinguish: ～が～なら、～も～だ (like parent, like child) vs ～も～なら、～も～だ (both sides are at fault) — two separate points; keep both
mistakes: Using it with verbs/adjectives: this pattern goes almost only with nouns. Incorrect: 忙しいが忙しいなら… → Avoid.
Understanding "なら" as an ordinary condition; here it is an evaluation of capacity/character, not "if…, then…".
Wrong core particle: using は instead of が/も loses the formulaic nuance. Prefer "NがNなら、NもNだ／NもNなら、NもNだ".
Using it in formal situations with the people directly involved can be rude because of its critical nuance.
JLPT: choose the correct order of the related noun pair (親–子, 師–弟…), and choose the ending だ (do not change it to ～ている...).

Going too far, there are limits

Each side has its own reasons/difficulties

examples: Love is the true source of strength, but it is hard to express.
Effort is the very key to success, but keeping it up is even harder.
Dialogue is the real way to a solution, but sorting out one's feelings takes time.
Now is the time for change, but without preparation it will lead to chaos.
Trust is the very foundation of cooperation, but once lost, it is hard to regain.
fields.explain:
Position: こそ comes right after the noun to be emphasized; then an affirmation with Nだ, followed by the conjunction が .
Nuance: strong emphasis in the first clause; the second clause is realistic, cautious, or a warning.
Pragmatics: suitable when balancing ideals and reality, or praising with a condition attached.
Formality: usable in both spoken and written language; add です／ます for politeness.

The pattern NこそNだが、～ puts absolute focus on the first clause (affirming "it is precisely…"), then uses が to present a reality, limitation or difficulty in the second clause. Natural reading: "It is true that N is indeed N, but…".
• こそ creates a strong "spotlight", affirming the target in the first clause unmistakably.
• …だが、 signals a contrastive turn: it acknowledges the value of A but points out B as an obstacle/exception.
• Often used in commentary, speeches and argumentative slogans: emphasis → turn to reality.
fields.notes:
• This pattern often appears in arguments that "praise a core value" but stress "the conditions for realizing it".
• The first clause can use abstract nouns: 愛・努力・信頼・自由・責任… to add weight.
• If the second clause only gives a mild warning, が can be replaced with けれど(も) to soften it.
mistakes: Mistaking が for the subject particle → here が is a contrastive conjunction that comes after だ.
Putting こそ in the wrong place (after a verb/adjective) → this pattern needs a noun as the core of emphasis.
A second clause that contradicts too strongly "completely negates" the first clause → the meaning becomes unbalanced; it should be a reasonable exception/difficulty.
Dropping だ before が in standard written language → with nouns, use Nだが、 for coherence.

rows: It is N that is N (absolute affirmation)
No contrastive clause; ends at the affirmation.
<ruby>努力<rt>どりょく</rt></ruby>こそ<ruby>成功<rt>せいこう</rt></ruby>だ。 Effort is what success truly is.
Adds a second clause stating a difficulty/condition/exception.
<ruby>愛<rt>あい</rt></ruby>こそ<ruby>力<rt>ちから</rt></ruby>だが、<ruby>難<rt>むずか</rt></ruby>しい。 Love is strength, but it is difficult.
Argumentative concession, without the spotlight emphasis of こそ.
<ruby>重要<rt>じゅうよう</rt></ruby>だとはいえ、<ruby>費用<rt>ひよう</rt></ruby>が<ruby>問題<rt>もんだい</rt></ruby>だ。 Although it is important, cost is the problem.
Formal written language; close to が but more refined.
<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>だものの、<ruby>準備<rt>じゅんび</rt></ruby><ruby>不足<rt>ふそく</rt></ruby>だ。 Although it is necessary, the preparation is insufficient.

examples: He dashed off like the wind.
A fragility like that of spring snow.
I felt as if I were in a dream.
Someone as humble as I cannot possibly take on such an important role.
This is not a job that the likes of him can do.
The rumor spread throughout the town like a spreading fire.
fields.explain:
Written language, speeches, literature; in speech ～ように／～みたいに is usually used.
When modifying a noun: prefer NのごときN. With pronouns/personal references it can be used directly:私ごとき.
"Xごときが/に" can easily sound insulting when said about others; consider the context.

• Comparison/metaphor: "like/similar to/as if". Has a literary, formal nuance.
• ごとき: modifies nouns; ごとく: modifies verbs/adjectives/whole clauses as an adverbial.
• Social nuance: "Xごときが/に" can be contemptuous when said about others; "私ごとき" is humble self-reference.
• かのごとく emphasizes "just as if" (even though it is not actually so).
fields.notes:
• "がごとく" has a classical flavor, often seen in titles/novels: ～するがごとく.
• Fixed rhetorical sequence: まるで／さながら＋V（か）のごとく.
• Function: ごとき（連体） ~ like an attributive adjective; ごとく (連用) ~ like an adverb.
mistakes: Dropping "の" carelessly: most cases need NのごときN; exceptions such as 私ごとき do not need の.
Using it about others causes offense: ×君ごときが口を出すな（strong, easily impolite).
Confusing it with spoken ように in exam questions: choose ごとく／ごとき when the context is formal/rhetorical.

rows: Close in meaning to "かのごとく", more commonly used
<ruby>氷<rt>こおり</rt></ruby>の<ruby>上<rt>うえ</rt></ruby>にいるかのようだ。
Formal, with a rhetorical, contemptuous or self-deprecating nuance

examples: Even without saying much, his resolve comes across.
I enlarged the diagram so that it can be understood without explanation.
Even without seeing the actual item, you can imagine how good the quality is.
Life is not so easy that you can succeed without making an effort.
There's no need to meet; email is enough.
fields.explain:
Often used to emphasize that something is obvious/sufficient, or to negate the expectation that one "must V".
More formal than ～なくても; suited to written language, headlines and declarations.
Can be combined with emphatic adverbs: わざわざ・いちいち + V-ずとも.

• "Even without V-ing / Even if you don't need to V, ... still ..."; emphasizes that condition A is not needed for B to happen.
• Used in arguments, written language and slogans; has a stiff, formal or rhetorical nuance.
• Often used with verbs of perception/ability: 分かる・伝わる・見える・言える・足りる.
fields.notes:
• ～とも here has the concessive meaning "even if ..., ...". Combined with "ず" (written negative), it gives a formal feel.
• Common in newspaper headlines/advertising: "登録せずとも使える".
• With verbs of perception, the subject is usually omitted: "言わずとも伝わる".
mistakes: Confusing it with ～ずに: ～ずに describes a sequence of actions and does not mean "even without ..., still ...".
Forgetting to change する → せずとも; writing "しずとも" is incorrect.
Using it in casual conversation can sound affected; the JLPT often tests its formal nuance compared with ～なくても.
